analysis.one_liner: Requires a court order before the government searches Americans' communications and bans forced encryption backdoors.
analysis.headline: Despite 42 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close two surveillance practices exposed after the Snowden disclosures. First, it would bar federal officials from searching through collections of communications gathered under foreign-surveillance authority in order to find a particular American's messages, unless a court order, an emergency, or the person's consent allows it. Second, it would prohibit federal agencies from forcing companies that make phones, computers, and software to build weaknesses into their products so the government can surveil users. It died without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose calls and emails are swept up when the government collects communications targeting people abroad, plus the public at large, whose devices and software would stay secure against government-mandated weaknesses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans whose communications get swept into surveillance

how_it_helps.text: No federal officer or employee could search a collection of communications acquired under Section 702 of FISA to find the communications of a particular U.S. person, unless that person is already subject to a surveillance court order, their life or safety is threatened, or they consent [S3].
The same warrant-style protection would extend to Americans' communications retained under intelligence collection activities not authorized by a court order, subpoena, or similar legal process [S2].

Federal agencies could not require or request makers of consumer computer hardware, software, or electronic devices to alter their security functions to allow surveillance of users or physical search of the product, with a narrow exception for mandates under the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence and law-enforcement agencies, which would lose the ability to search foreign-surveillance databases for Americans' communications on demand and could no longer compel tech companies to build surveillance access into their products.

drawbacks.text: Counterterrorism investigators argued that requiring a court order or an existing warrant before searching for an American inside foreign-intelligence collections would slow or block investigations, since targets abroad often communicate with people inside the United States [S2].

The protections contain carve-outs: corporations get no protection from warrantless searches at all, and agencies keep a path to mandate surveillance access under the Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act [S3].
The emergency exception lets agencies search without a warrant whenever they claim a person's life or safety is threatened, which critics could argue is a broad opening [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial for anyone who uses a phone or the internet: it ends warrantless government searches of Americans' communications and keeps consumer products from being deliberately weakened. The cost falls on intelligence operations, which would need court orders or existing warrants for searches targeting Americans, softened by emergency and consent exceptions. The main design weakness is that corporations are excluded from protection, even though businesses are frequent targets of surveillance data requests.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Intelligence and Judiciary committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee a month later, and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action before the 114th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Representative Ted Poe introduced the bill on May 5, 2015, joined by Representatives Zoe Lofgren and Thomas Massie as original cosponsors [S3].
The Speaker sent it to two committees at once, the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and the Judiciary Committee, rather than a single panel [S5].
On June 1, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations [S5].
That subcommittee referral was the last recorded action; the bill received no markup, no committee vote, and no House floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].
It attracted 42 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 28 Republicans, a bipartisan bloc, but bipartisan cosponsorship never translated into a hearing or vote [S4].

Congress did rework surveillance law that session, passing the narrower USA Freedom Act in June 2015, but that law did not include this bill's ban on warrantless backdoor searches or on encryption mandates (widely reported).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Intelligence agencies kept the power to search foreign-surveillance collections for Americans' communications without a court order, and the government kept the legal ability to pressure tech companies to build surveillance access into consumer products. Tech users and companies whose products could have been weakened gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies kept warrantless search authority

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the three named sponsors included two Republicans and a Democrat, and the 42 cosponsors split 28 Republicans to 14 Democrats [S4].

industries.industry: Intelligence agencies and the federal surveillance apparatus
industries.note: The bill would bar warrantless searches of Americans' communications in foreign-surveillance collections and end agency power to compel weakened product security. These agencies' interest in broad collection authority runs against the privacy interest of ordinary people, which is why the bill targets them.

Section 4 would shield makers of phones, computers, and software from government demands to build surveillance weaknesses into their products, a protection the industry had sought after the Snowden disclosures. Stronger default security also protects the customers who buy the products.
